newsitem.title: USA: US July CPI meets expectations for mild inflation.
newsitem.headline: US July CPI meets expectations for mild inflation.

text.p: U.S. consumer prices rose only modestly in July, signalling that inflation pressures remain subdued and providing leeway for the Federal Reserve to hold off on additional interest rate hikes in the near-term, economists said.

The Labor Department reported on Thursday that overall and core consumer prices rose a mild 0.2 percent in July, precisely in line with Wall Street expectations. The numbers came on the heels of another surprisingly benign inflation report on Wednesday which showed that producer prices declined for a record seventh consecutive month in July.
"It appears that both the CPI and PPI have bought some more time for the Fed," said Asha Bangalore, economist at Northern Trust Co.

Airline fares, which climbed 2.3 percent in July after a 1.2 percent decline in June showed the largest increase among sectors. Home fuel oil and gasoline declined by 1.9 percent and 0.4 percent, respectively, after substantial declines in the prior month as well.
Economists were cheered by an unchanged reading in medical care prices, which had been expected to rise again after a 0.2 percent increase in June.

"These numbers are telling us there is no near-term inflation," said Anthony Chan, chief economist at Banc One Investment Advisors Corp. "Medical care prices really stabilized and that is somewhat favorable."

On a year-over-year basis, consumer prices have risen a modest 2.2 percent, while core prices have advanced at a 2.4 percent pace -- confoundingly low numbers given the tight nature of U.S. labor markets and strength of the U.S. economy.
Expectations of strong third quarter consumption figures have economists wary of a robust rebound from trend-growth levels in the second quarter.
But without any concrete signs that inflation is picking up, some economists believe the Fed can afford to tolerate stronger growth before tightening credit.

The Federal Reserve will meet to decide the fate of short-term interest rates on August 19. It last raised rates on March 25, when the federal funds rate was pushed up 25 basis points to its current 5.50 percent.

"The August 19 decision now seems like foregone conclusion for steady policy," said Bangalore. "But if you look at the demand numbers you do have renewed strength after the pause in the second quarter, so I would think the Fed might have enough data by later this year to consider further action."
